title: What a p-value can and can't tell you
sub: Thousands of simulated experiments, with and without a real effect.

frames.caption: Run the same experiment 2,000 times: two groups of 50, compare their means, compute a p-value. Here the null is true: the groups come from the same distribution. The p-values are spread evenly from 0 to 1, so about 5% land below 0.05 (red). That 5% is the Type I error rate, by construction. Measured: 5.7%.

Now the treatment really works, with a small effect (0.2 standard deviations). The p-values pile up near 0, but most still land above 0.05: this study has only about 17% power. Most experiments miss a real effect.

A medium effect (0.5 standard deviations): about 71% of experiments reach p < 0.05. Same test, same α; what changed is the effect, and with it the power. A single p-value tells you which bar you landed in, not which world you are in.

scenarios.name: Peeking

frames.caption: No effect at all: 20 A/A tests where both arms are identical. Each line is a test's z-statistic, recomputed after every new observation. Outside the dashed lines, p < 0.05. A tester who peeks stops the first time a line crosses (red from then on).
A z-statistic under the null wanders. Checking it once, at a planned sample size, it is outside ±1.96 only 5% of the time. Checking it 100 times gives it 100 chances.
More lines have crossed at some point, even though nothing is going on. Many drift back inside later, but a peeker has already stopped and declared victory.

11 of these 20 null tests crossed at least once. Across 2,000 simulated tests, peeking after every observation from n = 10 to 100 gives a false positive rate of 27%, and to 1,000 gives 45%, against the advertised 5%. Keep going forever and every test crosses eventually. Sequential designs (alpha spending, always-valid p-values) fix this by raising the bar for early looks.

legend: after a peeker would have stopped
